title: The maker’s reason to pay.
body:
Patina · Furniture commerce research

The maker’s
reason to pay.

What brings a workshop or manufacturer onto Patina—and what makes the business worth keeping?

Customer evidence. Buying triggers. Priced offers. Seller returns. A 36-month operating model.

Internal decision deck · October 13, 2026 · All scenarios in USD

The test: sell one outcome that a budget owner can measure.
note: This revision investigates a business rather than merely presenting product concepts. The team researched current official trade programs, competitor pricing and financial reporting. No customer interviews were conducted and no company shown is claimed as a Patina prospect. Published capabilities are evidence; willingness to pay, conversion, retention and financial projections remain explicit test assumptions. The model starts with zero merchant accounts and zero active designer demand. It excludes existing Patina revenue and costs except where a proposed incremental budget is named.

title:
Sell a better trade operation.
Earn distribution afterward.
body:
First paying customer

A trade-ready collection maker with repeat requests, controlled options, and a person responsible for quotes.

First paid outcome

Fewer incomplete requests and corrections between the designer’s specification and maker acceptance.

Business condition

The maker renews for existing-account utility. New demand becomes a separate, attributed value test.
note: This recommendation is conditional. Small makers can be service-heavy; enterprise manufacturers can require long, bespoke integration projects. Start with frequency and repeatability rather than headcount. Pricing must be demonstrated through paid pilots. If interviews show makers only want customers, do not camouflage a demand-generation business as workflow software. Current Patina strategy is studio-first; maker subscriptions would expand the customer definition. The adopted V14 trade-margin policy must be reconciled before commercial offers.
question: Which outcome can the maker prove without relying on a promised audience?
source: Judgment from primary research; no validated Patina willingness-to-pay data.

title:
A website and trade pricing
are already inexpensive.
body:
Shopify Basic

$39 / month

US monthly billing. Basic B2B now includes company profiles and up to three active market catalogs.

$29 monthly equivalent when billed annually. Apps and implementation can add cost.

JOOR

Quote-based

Wholesale software with no order commission or exclusivity requirement; payments have separate fees.

Roomle

€1,150 / month

Annual-billing equivalent for its product configurator. Furniture rules, pricing, BOM, and integrations.

Euro license price, taxes excluded; digitization and scope need separate quotes.
note: Shopify changed its B2B entitlement in April 2026; simple trade selling is no longer Plus-only. Plus retains advanced features including unlimited catalogs, direct company/location assignment and deposits. Roomle’s cited plan is one website/domain with ten configurators; do not assume a license can be pooled across maker websites. JOOR does not publish a universal numeric brand price. These substitutes establish a baseline, not what any maker will pay Patina. Do not add their prices together into a fictional incumbent bundle.
question: What does the additional Patina bill buy that these tools do not already do well?
source: S01 · Shopify US pricing S02 · Shopify B2B plan entitlements S05 · JOOR pricing model S06 · Roomle Rubens pricing S25 · Shopify native B2B, April 2026

very different trade channels.

title:
Screen for work frequency
and buying authority.
body:
Independent workshop

Buyer: owner.
Trigger: repeated inquiries or an empty bench.
Veto: too few quotes, full capacity, every job unique.

May buy one-time publishing help before recurring software.

Trade-ready collection maker

Buyer: owner/GM or trade-sales lead.
Trigger: quotes exceed coordinator capacity.
Veto: weak data or no measurable recurring cost.

Recommended interview cohort; buyer roles remain to verify.

Established manufacturer

Buyer: sales leadership with IT and finance.
Trigger: funded channel or integration project.
Veto: dealer conflict and custom implementation.

Require paid discovery before enterprise commitments.
note: Proposed screen: existing designer accounts, repeatable furniture families, documented options, a named catalog owner, sufficient quote volume and room for profitable orders. Thirty to sixty quote events a month is an interview hypothesis, not a segment average or verified market distribution. Employee count alone is a poor signal. The owner can be both budget owner and working user in a small maker, but confirm that rather than treating enthusiasm from a sales associate as purchase authority.
question: Who can sign, what budget would fund it, and which current work or expense would change?

title:
Charge for a result
the buyer can inspect.
body:
Paid result hypothesisEvidence before the saleRenewal evidence
Faster accepted quotesBaseline touches and staff minutes on recent ordersComparable quotes need less total work
Fewer expensive correctionsActual remake, freight, or service invoicesVerified avoidable errors decline
Better existing-account serviceNamed studio requests and current response timeStudios reuse the agreed specification
Profitable new customersOriginal channel, capacity, and order contributionFulfilled incremental orders after fees
note: Separate four ledgers. Time freed is capacity value unless a paid expense falls. Avoided errors require a baseline and do not count rework twice if it is already inside order margin. Faster quotes are not automatically more sales: test whether the delay was actually losing orders. New customers are not necessarily incremental sales if they would have arrived anyway. A request, accepted quote, deposit and fulfilled order are different stages. A success metric should name the stage and denominator.
question: What would the budget owner show finance to defend renewal?

title:
The strongest invitation arrives
when the current process breaks.
body:
Triggers to recruit against

First hire

The owner needs someone else to quote without guessing.

New collection

Options, assets, and trade terms need a shared record.

Returned PO

Missing dimensions or receiver details delayed acceptance.

New territory

A rep needs a reliable assortment and attribution.

The approval chain

Working user → internal champion → budget owner → operations / systems approval.

Ask about the last software purchase: who approved it, how long it took, and what evidence mattered.

Owner-led purchasing and enterprise procurement need different sales motions.
note: These are specific recruiting hypotheses, not observed trigger rates. A workshop already booked for six months may want fewer unsuitable inquiries rather than more leads. A manufacturer with a mature portal may only consider Patina during an integration budget cycle. Ask which trigger is active now, how the maker currently responds, and whether there is authority and budget to act. Avoid treating a trade-show conversation as a qualified buying opportunity.
question: What event makes this purchase urgent enough to displace another priority?

title:
Offer a bounded outcome
at a written price.
body:
Assisted collection

$149 / month

Test range: $99–199.
Setup: $600 hypothesis.
A branded collection and structured inquiries.

Small workshop offer. Needs very low recurring service effort.

Connected trade desk

$299 / month

Setup: $995 hypothesis.
One collection, trade terms, quotes, approved editions, and project handoff.

Core projection assumes this price; willingness is unproven.

Attributed distribution

8% scenario

Optional share on eligible fulfilled merchandise, under agreed trade economics.

Free discovery profile could be tested separately. Combined adoption is not assumed proven.
note: These are price experiments, not a public rate card or verified willingness-to-pay. The first pilot can charge $500, credited toward a disclosed $995 setup amount if it continues; bill the disclosed subscription when usable, rather than charge twice for setup. Scope one collection with a capped number of families and clear rights to publish. Existing-account software utility and acquisition value should be sold and evaluated separately. Eight percent is a model input for the effective share of eligible merchandise, not an approved extra commission on top of V14. A free distribution-only cohort needs its own model; it cannot be added to paying SaaS cohorts as if it had $299 revenue.
question: Will five budget owners pay this price for a live pilot using their own collection?
source: Proposed merchant product; manufacturer onboarding remains a placeholder. Prices are tests, not approved offers.

title:
Give the maker several doors
from one trusted collection.
body:
The maker’s authoritative collection

Product families, feasible options, assets, and current commercial terms.

Maker approves publishing and acceptance.
Owned website

Branded pages or an embedded trade doorway.

Designer project

Samples, specifications, and client decisions.

Rep / showroom

Private assortments and attributed follow-up.

Patina discovery

Opt-in matching to a suitable project.

Social / events

Product links lead to the correct inquiry path.
note: Presence helps buyers understand the maker; sales channels must move qualified demand. A custom domain, public search indexing, photography, product feeds and maker-controlled presentation could matter to workshops, but are proposed capabilities. Existing merchants can keep their site and commerce stack. Faire already documents Shopify synchronization and JOOR already connects digital showrooms with in-person selling. Patina must show why reuse inside the designer project improves the order. Before synchronization, choose the authoritative owner of each field and show a confirmation timestamp. A stale catalog shared five ways increases risk.
question: Which two doors can share a product record without adding maintenance?
source: S30 · Faire Shopify synchronization S31 · JOOR virtual showrooms

title:
Join around the next live quote,
then expand the collection.
body:
Bring a request

A designer inquiry and the maker’s current process.

Prepare a family

Import assets and rules; flag missing facts.

Maker confirms

Options, trade access, lead-time semantics.

Quote together

Sample, revision, seller acceptance.

Reuse it

Maker and studio carry the same record onward.

Assisted setup removes initial work. Recurring value must survive after Patina’s assistance stops.
note: Proposed activation means a maker-approved product family, a named data owner, and a real accepted quote reused by a designer—not an account created or photos uploaded. An import is a draft; generated product facts, prices and feasible configurations require maker confirmation. A first useful product family can be prepared without populating the entire catalog. Use maker-held payments initially and do not require replacing an ERP. Manufacturer onboarding currently remains a placeholder in repository evidence; the deck does not claim this joining flow is implemented.
question: What can the maker do unaided on the second request?

title: Setup has costs on both sides.
body:
Core scenario assumptionMaker’s burdenPatina’s delivery burden
Upfront setupPay $995; spend 8 internal hours8 delivery hours × $45 = $360
Recurring upkeep1.5 hours/month to maintain facts1.5 service hours/month + $12 tools
Collection feePart of the software invoice3% revenue allowance in model
Scope boundaryOne collection; human custom approvalData repair and ERP work scoped separately
note: The maker’s eight hours and Patina’s eight hours are separate assumptions; do not hide either as free labor. Maker internal labor is allocated across twelve months in its value model. Patina setup contribution is $995 less $29.85 collection allowance and $360 delivery labor, or $605.15, before acquisition and fixed costs. Those hours must include mapping, permissions, training and checking a real quote. The customer research shows onboarding can erase a small maker’s benefit. Template cleanup and valid configuration rules are the work; a file upload is not completion.
question: If setup takes twenty hours, does the price—or the customer—need to change?
source: A04–A07: test assumptions. Pilot logs must replace them.

title:
At $299, the ordinary case
still needs to prove its value.
body:
Thirty quotes per month

30 minutes removed per quote creates 15 hours of capacity. At $45/hour and 50% documented cost realization: $338.

0.18 fee-eligible orders × 60% incrementality yields 0.108 additional orders. At 30% contribution, less the 8% fee on all eligible orders: $72.

Full first-year monthly burden

Subscription$299
Setup + maker effort, spread over 12 months$113
Catalog upkeep$68
Monthly value surplus−$70
note: This is a reconciled illustration, not measured customer value. The base platform scenario yields about 0.18 eligible completed orders per maker in month 36; a further 60% causal-incrementality assumption gives roughly 0.10 additional orders. Fees apply to every eligible order, including the 40% assumed to have occurred anyway; those fees are deducted without incremental contribution. Thirty quotes saving thirty minutes, $45 labor and 50% cost realization remain assumptions. Realization requires an identifiable reduced expense, otherwise report capacity only. Extra orders must have production capacity and contribution after incremental material, labor, freight, payment and warranty cost. Do not reuse the same recovered hours as both labor savings and production value. A busier maker or lower price may work; the ordinary illustration is a reason to test, not to claim a positive ROI.
question: Which measured input makes this account worth paying for: volume, cost removal, errors, or demand?
source: A13 seller value model. Outputs rounded; full assumptions and arithmetic are downloadable.

title:
Change the inputs.
See when the maker should decline.
body:
Fixed illustration: $4,000 order; 8% eligible fee; $45/hour; $995 setup; 8 maker setup hours spread over 12 months; 1.5 upkeep hours/month.

Capacity value (not automatically cash)
Realized cost removal
Incremental order contribution after fee
Subscription + setup allocation + upkeep
Monthly customer value surplus
note: Use actual order records and paid expenses to replace every assumption. Cost realization at zero removes labor cash value entirely; the freed hours can still be useful capacity. The eligible-order input is completed attributed business. Incrementality estimates what would otherwise not have occurred. Contribution accrues only to incremental orders, while fees apply to all eligible orders. The 30% contribution assumption is not taken from reported manufacturer gross margins. Upkeep and maker setup effort are economic costs valued at the assumed labor rate, so this is a customer value-surplus model rather than an audited cash-flow statement. No forecast of avoided remakes is included without evidence.
question: Would this maker renew if incremental orders were zero for six months?

title:
Agree whose customer it is
before deciding what to charge.
body:
Relationship / purchaseOffer hypothesisRule to settle
Maker brings its existing accountSoftware utility; no new-demand fee in this proposalExisting V14 order terms remain separately governed
Patina originates eligible businessEffective 8% retained share in the modelAttribution evidence, window, exclusions, repeat treatment
Rep or showroom already owns accountPreserve the existing partner’s roleTerritory, introduced project, correction process
Maker chooses both productsSubscription + eligible share only if both earn valueNo undisclosed stacking of charges
note: Current V14 says Patina margin is carved from maker trade discount while studio markup remains intact. This proposal does not authorize an additional blanket fee on top of that margin. The model’s 8% is a hypothetical effective platform share of eligible net merchandise under an agreed or renegotiated arrangement. Existing-account orders serviced by software are excluded from new-demand GMV. Determine seller identity, merchandise value denominator, fee basis, repeat-order treatment, and representative compensation before any pilot order with a commercial fee. The maker can pay for the trade desk without claiming Patina brought the buyer. A relationship correction must have an evidence process.
question: Does Patina earn a fee for the introduction, coordination, or every repeat order?
source: S03 · Faire North American fees S04 · Faire Direct eligibility · Patina V14: Vision decisions

title:
A percentage fee can consume
a large share of the maker’s profit.
body:
Illustrative $4,000 merchandise order30% incremental contribution15% incremental contribution
Contribution before Patina fee$1,200$600
8% eligible share$320$320
Contribution remaining$880$280
Share of pre-fee contribution consumed27%53%
Reported gross margins vary: Hooker Domestic Upholstery FY2026 18.3%; MillerKnoll consolidated FY2026 38.8%. Neither is a small-maker contribution benchmark.
note: The order example assumes contribution after incremental production, packaging, freight subsidy, payment, warranty and selling costs, before the proposed Patina share. Existing trade-discount economics can make the counterfactual different; use the maker’s actual net proceeds. Hooker’s period ended February 1, 2026 and includes a different domestic upholstery business; MillerKnoll’s period ended May 30, 2026 and is consolidated across channels. MillerKnoll’s GAAP operating margin was 5.2%. The reported figures show why gross margin cannot establish fee affordability. Faire’s cited North American schedule is 15% plus $10 first order and separate processing; its value and risk allocation differ. Do not claim an 8% Patina offer is universally cheaper.
question: At what order contribution does this fee stop making sense?
source: S20 · Hooker FY2026 financial results S21 · MillerKnoll FY2026 financial results S03 · Faire North American fees

title:
More makers do not create
more rooms to furnish.
body:
100 active designer accounts

Assume 0.4 sourcing projects/month × 50% category fit × 50% order conversion × 1.1 pieces × 85% fulfillment × 75% fee eligibility.

7 eligible orders / month

At $4,000 merchandise value and 8% effective share: about $2,244 revenue/month.

What must become real

A current project. Relevant supply. A maker-accepted quote. A fulfilled order. Defensible attribution.

Designer signups, maker uploads, sample requests, and competing quotes are earlier stages.

This illustration excludes lag; the cohort model includes it.
note: All numeric conversion inputs are hypotheses. Active designer accounts means accounts producing sourcing opportunities at the assumed frequency, not app logins. The conversion denominator is an eligible sourcing project, with a unique project identifier; multiple quotes for one purchase are not multiple orders. The model caps accepted orders by maker supply capacity, applies a two-month fulfillment lag and completion factor, and only earns fees on an eligible share of fulfilled merchandise. Attribution is not proof of causal incrementality. In the base month-36 case, eligible orders per paying maker remain modest and uneven; do not promise each maker one new order a month.
question: How many real, category-relevant projects can Patina bring in the next quarter?
source: A08–A10: demand assumptions. Starts at zero; no existing Patina audience is presumed.

title:
The base funnel yields
2.7 activations from 60 contacts.
body:
60 named accounts

Unique suitable businesses contacted per month.

15 qualified

25% fit and budget-owner qualification.

6 pilots

40% proceed to a bounded trial.

3 accept offer

50% choose the disclosed continuation.

2.7 activate

90% usable after a two-month lag.

Modeled acquisition cost

$922 / activation

$28 per contacted account + three pilot hours at $45. Failed pilots are included.

The list is an assumption too

60 / 100 / 160 contacts per month across years requires 3,840 distinct suitable accounts.

No researched count proves that reachable pool exists. Regional success would need broader expansion.
note: Expected activation is fractional for scenario arithmetic; actual cohorts will contain whole businesses with more variation. The $28 contact cost covers research, outreach and qualification labor; three pilot hours cover guided testing, while eight onboarding hours are post-sale delivery. This prevents double-counting the same activity. CAC here excludes onboarding, which is separately offset by setup fee, and includes failed trials. Do not reinterpret a repeated follow-up as a new unique account. Before extrapolating years two and three, build a named reachable list, deduplicate parent companies, and record qualification/refusal reasons.
question: Can the team name the first sixty plausibly suitable accounts rather than purchase a large generic list?

title:
A useful introduction beats
a generic marketplace invitation.
body:
Acquisition route to testConcrete reason to joinMeasurement
Designer nomination“Make the next quote for this studio easier.”Qualified owner meeting → paid pilot
Rep / showroom partnerA private collection and preserved account creditIntroductions, activation, partner disputes
Collection launch serviceTurn a real line sheet into usable product familiesSetup hours, paid continuation, upkeep
Targeted event follow-upOne known product family and one live workflow gapAll-in event cost / paid activations
note: High Point publishes a searchable exhibitor directory and program materials; that is a route to research, not permission to assume leads or conversions. The first cohort should use direct relationships where available, without claiming a scalable network exists. A rep channel might lower contact cost but add referral compensation, territory requirements and complexity; those partner costs are not baked into the current base acquisition model. Events can produce many conversations but high all-in CAC once travel and founder time are included. Run channels separately and compare retained paid activations.
question: Which channel brings budget owners with live work—and what does a retained account cost?
source: S23 · High Point exhibitor directory S26 · Material Bank representative resources

title:
The next order should be easier
because the last one happened here.
body:
Keep useful memory

Maker-confirmed options, accepted editions, samples, and revision history.

Keep trusted relationships

Clear account ownership, rep credit, and an exportable record to build.

Keep current facts

A named owner and confirmation date for prices, inventory, and timing.

Renewal evidence: repeated real requests, less total work, stable catalog upkeep, and satisfactory order outcomes.
note: A specification record alone is copyable. Defensibility would need repeated cross-company adoption and a history participants trust. Data rights and practical exportability are design requirements to build, not current promises. Paid retention cannot be inferred from usage during a hands-on pilot. At monthly maker churn of 1.5%, only about 83.4% of a cohort remains after twelve months even without downgrades. Source freshness can increase workload and churn; test maintenance as seriously as the initial demo. The contract must let the maker leave without making ordinary work impossible.
question: What disappears from the maker’s work if they cancel—and is that loss worth the bill?

title:
Cohorts drive subscriptions.
Completed, eligible orders drive fees.
body:
Active makers[t] = retained makers[t−1]
+ successful activations from the earlier funnel
Accepted orders = min(project demand, maker capacity)
Fulfilled orders = accepted queue × completion rate
Eligible fee revenue = fulfilled merchandise
× attributable share × effective retained rate

Collection and staffing rules

Bill software/setup on activation. Collect fulfillment fees one month later. Pay modeled costs in the month incurred.

Maker holds merchandise payments. Patina neither books GMV as revenue nor funds furniture production.

Variable delivery contractors are separate from the fixed product/engineering team.
note: The model is monthly for 36 months with explicit queues. Activations bill a full month; pre-activation costs are inside acquisition and pilot budgets. Accepted orders can remain in the fulfillment queue even if software accounts later churn. Failed orders still incur accepted-order coordination labor; fulfilled GMV bears an additional 0.5% service/refund reserve allowance. Only eligible merchandise contributes platform fee revenue. Software, setup and fee invoices are collected in full on the stated schedule; bad debt, taxes, capex, payment custody and inventory financing are excluded. This is a conditional planning cash schedule, not audited company cash flow. Every output is reproducible from a single model implementation.
question: What would change if Patina collected the deposit or guaranteed delivery?

Marketplace fees remain a minority.

title:
See the cash trough
before choosing the growth plan.
body:
Cumulative net cash after the $60,000 initial build. No financing injected.
Year 3 revenue
Year 3 operating result
Peak modeled cash deficit
Sustained monthly operating break-even

note: Sustained break-even means every modeled remaining month has a nonnegative operating result; one positive month before the fixed-cost step-up is not sufficient. Cumulative cash recovery includes initial build and the one-month collection delay for fee invoices. Peak deficit assumes all modeled invoices collect on schedule and all costs pay when incurred. It excludes tax, capex, bad debt, merchandise deposits, maker liabilities and a management contingency. A planning reserve of twenty percent would add buffer but is not embedded as operating cost. The current base model does not recover by month thirty-six. Use the source files to inspect each monthly row.
question: What is the maximum committed downside before the next decision gate?

title:
Good account contribution
does not guarantee company profit.
body:
Per retained maker / month

$211

$299 subscription − $8.97 billing − $67.50 service − $12 tools.

Excludes buyer service, acquisition, marketplace coordination, and fixed costs.

Acquisition payback

4.4 months

$922 acquisition cost / $210.53 recurring contribution.

No setup credit or transaction revenue assumed in this payback.

Cohort retention

83.4% / year

Implied by 1.5% monthly maker churn.

Not observed retention. Furniture cycles require 90- and 180-day checks.
note: Do not market this as proven CAC or LTV. CAC divides total acquisition and guided-pilot cost by successfully activated accounts; zero activation makes CAC undefined. Subscription payback uses contribution before fixed costs and separate buyer-side expenses. Setup contribution is $605.15 before acquisition, not a recurring subsidy. A shorter payback can coexist with an operating loss because the business pays engineering, product, buyer acquisition and support for a growing network. Monthly churn is an assumption, and its twelve-month retention compound is calculated rather than rounded as eighteen percent annual loss.
question: Can Patina keep service effort low while the maker still receives enough value?

title:
Price, service and adoption
can change the business more than GMV.
body: One input changes at a time; all other base assumptions remain fixed. Higher prices may reduce conversion, so this is arithmetic sensitivity—not causal evidence.
note: The sensitivity table is generated from the same model used for the projections. It compares a software-only case with no marketplace demand cost, the base, $149 and $399 subscription, doubled maker support, three-percent churn, halved designer additions and fifty-percent more maker contacts. Higher price leaves conversion unchanged for isolation, which is unlikely to hold automatically. More contacts also increases acquisition/pilot cost. Low marketplace fees should be negotiated against merchant value and platform cost rather than assumed as a growth lever. An attractive result from a single assumption change is a test agenda, not a forecast revision.
question: Which improvement is within Patina’s control—and which depends on a buyer choosing us?

title:
The model requires real people
behind the software.
body:
Base case at month 36

3.9 delivery equivalents

About 432 monthly service hours / 110 productive hours per delivery role.

Pilots, onboarding, maker upkeep, designer support, and order coordination are included.

Upside at month 36

9.2 delivery equivalents

About 1,015 monthly service hours, before core engineering, product, and outreach.

Variable delivery labor is already costed at $45/hour. Do not put it in the fixed budget again.
note: The 110 productive-hours allowance is a planning assumption for paid delivery capacity after meetings, leave and administrative time. It is not a labor productivity benchmark. The model assumes this capacity can be obtained flexibly at the stated loaded rate; permanent hires and utilization floors would alter cash costs. Fixed monthly budgets of $20k/$25k/$35k in base cover core product/engineering/overhead and exclude separately costed delivery and contact labor. Upside spends $25k/$35k/$50k fixed while requiring more variable service capacity. The most useful operational metric is hours per repeated account or accepted order, not an automation percentage.
question: Can the second and third orders reduce human work—or does every account remain a service project?
source: A04–A07, A12. Service capacity derived from the monthly model.

title:
The research leaves
three credible businesses to choose.
body:
Business centerWhy a maker paysWhat changes the economics
Trade desk softwareExisting relationships become easier to serveFrequency, renewal, low support, catalog upkeep
Attributed distributionProfitable customers it would not otherwise winDesigner demand, incrementality, order contribution
Enterprise integrationA measurable channel handoff fits its systemsContract value, sales cycle, customization burden
Storefronts, shared showrooms, capacity passports and room visualization can support these businesses. Each must earn its scope through the chosen customer’s outcome.
note: Do not choose the most imaginative feature as the company strategy. A standalone site builder competes with inexpensive horizontal tools and needs low service cost. A distributed showroom may strengthen existing reps but introduces partner and physical-service costs. A capacity exchange differentiates through production knowledge but intensifies delays and disputes. Advanced visual configuration is available from providers such as Roomle and Threekit; deployment rights and digitization economics matter. The recommended first trade desk can keep the other routes open without funding them all.
question: Which business would Patina be willing to operate through its difficult cases?
source: S06 · Roomle Rubens pricing S07 · RepSpark pricing S08 · Threekit pricing and asset ownership S28 · Roomle configurator capabilities

title:
Fund a buying test
before a broad product build.
body:
Phase / proposed spend gateWork and evidenceContinue only if…
First 2 weeks · up to $5k20 qualified budget-owner discussions; real order recordsFive accept a written paid pilot; recruit the next five within the existing $25k cap
Weeks 3–8 · next $20kOne collection each; live quote handoffs; timed workMedian setup ≤10h; maker and designer reuse unaided
Days 60–180 · release next tranche only on reviewDisclosed recurring price; fulfilled-order and renewal trackingSeven of ten renew after equivalent exposure; support trends toward ≤1.5h/account/mo
Proposed gates, not statistical proof. Start with a $25k commitment; the projection’s $60k initial build is conditional on passing staged review.
note: The pilot budget and thresholds are judgments for leadership to approve, not quoted implementation estimates. Twenty interviews must reach qualified economic buyers; sampling friendly users biases results. Payment, catalog access and a named data owner are stronger than stated interest. Completing a quote is not proof of a delivered order, so delivery and repeat behavior continue beyond the first eight weeks. Seven of ten renewals is a small learning signal; report every refusal and incentive rather than present it as a retention estimate. Preserve at least a day-90 and day-180 review before scaling acquisition. A failed downside test should stop spend; the three-year downside is intentionally a mechanical continuation stress case.
question: What evidence permits the next $25,000—and who can stop it?

title:
Ask for the last real order,
the last bill, and the next signature.
body:
The last order

Show inquiry, quote, revisions, payment and delivery. Where did work repeat?

The last error

What did the correction actually cost? Which part was preventable?

The last new buyer

Who introduced them, what did acquisition cost, and was the sale incremental?

The last bill

Which tool, contractor, overtime or selling expense did you pay?

The last purchase

Who approved software, what evidence mattered, and why did you cancel a tool?

The next commitment

Will the budget owner sign a scoped paid test and provide baseline records?
note: Request records with permission and limit them to what the analysis needs. Reconstruct the last ten requests rather than hand-pick one memorable success. Distinguish the user’s workflow pain from the budget owner’s purchasing criteria. When capacity is full, ask what work they declined or displaced and whether better qualification would help. Ask how a price change or maintenance task would alter the decision. Record no-purchase outcomes, including whether the current system is simply good enough. The full customer and commercial research files include detailed question sets; the slide concentrates the six document-based themes.
question: What finding would make us stop pursuing this segment?

title:
Settle the assumptions that
change the company we are building.
body:
DecisionA real choiceEvidence required
Who pays first?Small workshop vs trade-ready maker vs enterprisePaid intent, authority, event frequency
What earns the fee?Workflow vs new demand vs coordinationCost removal, incrementality, order economics
Who owns the order?Maker seller vs managed commerceContracts, support, cash and liability design
What scales first?Regional niche vs broader category/channelNamed supply list and active projects
How much to commit?Staged pilot vs $60k initial build + runwayGate owners, maximum loss, next review
note: Questions should produce a decision and an evidence request rather than invite abstract agreement. A budget owner should know what would pause or redirect the program. Current studio-first scope and V14 economics remain adopted until explicitly changed. The cohort model’s combined software and eligible-share adoption is a hypothesis; if the pilot only validates one product, rerun that business rather than keep the revenue from the unvalidated product. The business must also improve designer work enough to preserve Patina’s current customer promise.
question: Which assumption would overturn the recommended trade-desk entry point?

title:
Leave with an offer,
a disproof, and an owner.
body:
Recommended next action

Sell a bounded trade-desk pilot to collection makers already serving studios. Measure both sides’ work before promising new demand.

Test $149 versus $299 recurring offers against documented value. Keep $995 setup visible, including maker effort.

Pricing research should explain refusals, not hide them through free service.

The company earns permission to expand when a maker pays, uses it again, and renews with less help.

Saved locally where supported. Export keeps a complete copy.
note: The export includes the selected operating scenario and its assumptions as well as the discussion record. It stays in this browser and never submits to a server. A local-storage failure does not prevent export. Choose a maximum spend and a named date before proceeding. A prospective maker paying a low pilot fee can still be doing a favor; examine full-price renewal and unaided repeated use. The strongest learning outcome can be a decision to lower the price, change the segment, choose a distribution business, or pause.
